claim: Cerebellar climbing fiber activity encodes performance errors during many motor learning tasks.
source: Cerebellar climbing fiber activity encodes performance errors during many motor learning tasks, but the role of these error signals in learning has been controversial.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: During VOR-increase training, climbing fiber activity on one trial predicted changes in cerebellar output on the next trial.
source: During VOR-increase training, climbing fiber activity on one trial predicted changes in cerebellar output on the next trial, and optogenetic activation of climbing fibers to mimic their encoding of performance errors was sufficient to implant a motor memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C demonstrating trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber spikes and Purkinje cell output changes.

claim: Optogenetic activation of climbing fibers to mimic their encoding of performance errors was sufficient to implant a motor memory during VOR-increase training.
source: During VOR-increase training, climbing fiber activity on one trial predicted changes in cerebellar output on the next trial, and optogenetic activation of climbing fibers to mimic their encoding of performance errors was sufficient to implant a motor memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7 demonstrating that optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli induced VOR-increase learning.

claim: During VOR-decrease training, there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in cerebellar output.
source: In contrast, during VOR-decrease training, there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in cerebellar output, and climbing fiber activation did not induce VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E demonstrating the absence of correlation between climbing fiber spikes and Purkinje cell output changes during VOR-decrease training.

claim: Climbing fiber activation did not induce VOR-decrease learning.
source: In contrast, during VOR-decrease training, there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in cerebellar output, and climbing fiber activation did not induce VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7 demonstrating that optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation during contraversive vestibular stimuli did not induce VOR-decrease learning.

claim: The ability of climbing fibers to induce plasticity can be dynamically gated in vivo, even under conditions where climbing fibers are robustly activated by performance errors.
source: Our data suggest that the ability of climbing fibers to induce plasticity can be dynamically gated in vivo, even under conditions where climbing fibers are robustly activated by performance errors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training paradigms.

claim: The cerebellum implements a supervised learning algorithm, with the climbing fiber input providing error signals that induce learning.
source: The cerebellum is thought to implement a supervised learning algorithm, with the climbing fiber input to the cerebellum providing error signals that induce learning.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations to Marr, 1969 and Albus, 1971.

claim: Performance errors activate neurons in the inferior olive and their climbing fiber axons, which trigger the induction of plasticity in the cerebellar cortex to produce adaptive changes in behavior.
source: According to this model, performance errors activate neurons in the inferior olive and their climbing fiber axons, which in turn trigger the induction of plasticity in the cerebellar cortex to produce adaptive changes in behavior (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational theoretical work.

claim: The cerebellar learning process is regulated by a feedback loop from the cerebellar cortex to the inferior olive.
source: Previous work has shown that this process is regulated by a feedback loop from the cerebellar cortex to the inferior olive (Andersson and Armstrong, 1987; Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994; Medina et al., 2002; Rasmussen et al., 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2013; reviewed in Apps, 1999; Gibson et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Even when climbing fibers are robustly activated by performance errors, the ability of that climbing fiber activity to trigger plasticity can be regulated by the state of the cerebellar circuit.
source: In this study, we describe a second level of regulation in animals undergoing learning: even when climbing fibers are robustly activated by performance errors, the ability of that climbing fiber activity to trigger plasticity can be regulated by the state of the cerebellar circuit.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the experimental data comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.

claim: Climbing fibers are activated by performance errors during a wide range of motor learning tasks.
source: Climbing fibers are activated by performance errors during a wide range of motor learning tasks (for a review, see Ito, 2001), and several lines of evidence suggest that this provides a potent trigger for cerebellar plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A single spike in a climbing fiber reliably triggers a complex spike in its Purkinje cell targets.
source: A single spike in a climbing fiber reliably triggers a complex spike in its Purkinje cell targets (Eccles et al., 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eccles et al., 1966.

claim: Calcium transients associated with complex spikes can induce synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex in vitro.
source: Calcium transients associated with complex spikes can induce synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex in vitro (for reviews, see Hansel et al., 2001; Ito, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Climbing fiber activation can replace the unconditioned stimulus used to induce cerebellum-dependent classical conditioning in vivo.
source: In vivo, climbing fiber activation can replace the unconditioned stimulus used to induce a form of cerebellum-dependent classical conditioning (Mauk et al., 1986; Steinmetz et al., 1989; Jirenhed et al., 2007; Rasmussen et al., 2013) or the sensory feedback used to induce oculomotor learning (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fiber activation can replace the sensory feedback used to induce oculomotor learning.
source: In vivo, climbing fiber activation can replace the unconditioned stimulus used to induce a form of cerebellum-dependent classical conditioning (Mauk et al., 1986; Steinmetz et al., 1989; Jirenhed et al., 2007; Rasmussen et al., 2013) or the sensory feedback used to induce oculomotor learning (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013.

claim: During a smooth pursuit oculomotor learning task, there is a tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of individual spikes in a climbing fiber and changes in cerebellar output on the subsequent trial.
source: Moreover, during a smooth pursuit oculomotor learning task, there is a tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of individual spikes in a climbing fiber and changes in cerebellar output on the subsequent trial, suggesting that climbing fiber spikes provide a potent and reliable trigger for plasticity (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2010, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recordings during some cerebellum-dependent tasks have revealed a dissociation between the encoding of errors and the induction of learning over the course of a training session.
source: Recordings during some cerebellum-dependent tasks have revealed a dissociation between the encoding of errors and the induction of learning over the course of a training session (Catz et al., 2005; Ke et al., 2009; Kitazawa et al., 1998; Ojakangas and Ebner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Perturbation of long-term depression of the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD) impairs certain learning tasks while leaving other cerebellum-dependent learning tasks intact.
source: In addition, perturbation of the most extensively studied form of climbing fiber-triggered plasticity, long-term depression of the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD), impairs certain learning tasks while leaving other cerebellum-dependent learning tasks intact (Aiba et al., 1994; Boyden et al., 2006; De Zeeuw et al., 1998; Feil et al., 2003; Hansel et al., 2006; Katoh et al., 2000; Katoh et al, 2005; Kim and Thompson, 1997; Kishimoto et al., 2001; Kishimoto et al., 2001; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Schonewille et al., 2011; Shibuki et al., 1996; Shutoh et al., 2002, 2003; van Alphen and De Zeeuw, 2002; Welsh et al., 2005; Yanagihara and Kondo, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to previous studies.

claim: A Purkinje cell's response to its climbing fiber input can be graded, which can regulate the efficacy of climbing fiber stimulation to induce plasticity in vitro and in decerebrate preparations.
source: However, more recently, it has been shown that a Purkinje cell's response to its climbing fiber input can be graded, which, in turn, can regulate the efficacy of climbing fiber stimulation to induce plasticity in vitro and in decerebrate preparations (Weber et al., 2003; Carey and Regehr, 2009; Maruta et al, 2007; Mathy et al., 2009; Rasmussen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vestibular stimuli (head movements) drive eye movement responses through VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei.
source: Vestibular stimuli (head movements) drive eye movement responses through VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Vestibular signals are conveyed, via parallel fibers and interneurons, to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar floccular complex.
source: Vestibular signals are also conveyed, via parallel fibers and interneurons, to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar floccular complex.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Purkinje cells receive input from climbing fibers that respond to retinal slip, which indicates a performance error.
source: Purkinje cells also receive input from climbing fibers that respond to retinal slip, which indicates a performance error--a failure of eye movements to stabilize a visual image on the retina.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Climbing fiber activity is hypothesized to drive plasticity in the other inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: Climbing fiber activity is hypothesized to drive plasticity in the other inputs to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Changes in Purkinje cell output can influence eye movements through their inhibitory effect on VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei.
source: Changes in Purkinje cell output can influence eye movements through their inhibitory effect on VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber and each spike in that climbing fiber reliably triggers a complex spike in the Purkinje cell.
source: An extracellular recording from a Purkinje cell can detect complex spikes, which reflect spikes in its single climbing fiber input with a one-to-one correspondence, and simple spikes (71 ± 9 sp/s, mean ± SEM), which greatly outnumber complex spikes (0.98 ± 0.19 sp/s) and thus are the major output from the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1, and is supported by the citation to Eccles et al., 1966 elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Simple spikes greatly outnumber complex spikes and are the major output from Purkinje cells.
source: An extracellular recording from a Purkinje cell can detect complex spikes, which reflect spikes in its single climbing fiber input with a one-to-one correspondence, and simple spikes (71 ± 9 sp/s, mean ± SEM), which greatly outnumber complex spikes (0.98 ± 0.19 sp/s) and thus are the major output from the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with specific firing rate measurements and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: During VOR-increase training, the visual stimulus is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction.
source: During VOR-increase training (A), the visual stimulus (grey trace) is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction (red).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: During VOR-decrease training, the visual stimulus is paired with a vestibular stimulus moving in the same direction.
source: During VOR-decrease training (B), the visual stimulus is paired with a vestibular stimulus moving in the same direction (blue).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: During the visual-vestibular training stimuli, there is retinal slip, reflecting the failure of the eye movements to stabilize the visual stimulus.
source: During the visual-vestibular training stimuli, there is retinal slip, reflecting the failure of the eye movements to stabilize the visual stimulus, which is a performance error.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C,D.

claim: During VOR-increase training, the probability of a climbing fiber spike was elevated 75–250 ms after the onset of each ipsiversive vestibular stimulus.
source: During VOR-increase training (E), the probability of a climbing fiber spike was elevated in a window 75–250 ms (grey box) after the onset of each ipsiversive vestibular stimulus (i.e., climbing fiber activity in the left flocculus increased during head rotation to the left).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2E.

claim: During VOR-decrease training, climbing fibers increased their firing probability 75–250 ms after the onset of a contraversive vestibular stimulus.
source: During VOR-decrease training (F), the same climbing fibers increased their firing probability 75–250 ms after the onset of a contraversive vestibular stimulus.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: All climbing fibers that responded during VOR-increase training also responded during VOR-decrease training, with similar response amplitude.
source: All climbing fibers that responded during one training paradigm also responded during the other paradigm, and with a similar response amplitude (t(9) = 1.77, p=0.11 paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: The VOR functions to stabilize visual images on the retina by using vestibular signals to elicit eye movements that compensate for head movements.
source: The VOR functions to stabilize visual images on the retina by using vestibular signals to elicit eye movements that compensate for head movements.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the VOR.

claim: VOR gain calibration occurs through a form of motor learning that depends on the cerebellar floccular complex.
source: This calibration occurs through a form of motor learning that depends on the cerebellar floccular complex (flocculus and ventral paraflocculus) (Robinson, 1976; Ito et al., 1982; Lisberger et al, 1984; Nagao, 1983; McElligott et al., 1998; Rambold et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fibers in the floccular complex are robustly activated by performance errors during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning.
source: Climbing fibers in this part of the cerebellum are robustly activated by performance errors during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning: if the eye movements driven by the VOR are too small or too big, that performance error results in image motion on the retina (retinal slip), which is encoded by the floccular climbing fibers (Ghelarducci et al., 1975; Graf et al., 1988; Simpson and Alley, 1974; Stone and Lisberger, 1990; Figure 2C–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The same climbing fibers encode performance errors during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning.
source: The same climbing fibers encode performance errors during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing the same cells respond to both training paradigms.

claim: Over the course of both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning, the Purkinje cell simple spike output during the VOR is altered in a manner consistent with the induction of LTD in parallel fiber inputs that were coactive with the climbing fibers during training.
source: Over the course of both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning, the Purkinje cell simple spike output during the VOR is altered in a manner consistent with the induction of LTD in parallel fiber inputs that were coactive with the climbing fibers during training (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Direct, optogenetic activation of the climbing fibers can induce VOR-increase learning when paired with a vestibular stimulus.
source: Also, direct, optogenetic activation of the climbing fibers can induce VOR-increase learning, when paired with a vestibular stimulus (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A previous attempt to induce VOR-decrease learning with climbing fiber stimulation was unsuccessful.
source: On the other hand, a previous attempt to induce VOR-decrease learning with climbing fiber stimulation was unsuccessful (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies of multiple lines of mice deficient in pf-Pk LTD have not consistently found impairments of VOR learning, and the reported impairments are more pronounced for VOR-increase than VOR-decrease learning.
source: Moreover, studies of multiple lines of mice deficient in pf-Pk LTD have not consistently found impairments of VOR learning, and the reported impairments are more pronounced for VOR-increase than VOR-decrease learning (Aiba et al., 1994; Boyden et al., 2006; De Zeeuw et al., 1998; Feil et al., 2003; Hansel et al., 2006; Kim and Thompson, 1997; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Schonewille et al., 2011; van Alphen and De Zeeuw, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Recordings were made from 10 Purkinje cells in the flocculus and ventral paraflocculus of two awake, behaving, male rhesus monkeys.
source: We recorded from Purkinje cells in the floccular complex of two adult rhesus monkeys during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and data collection.

claim: An extracellular recording from a Purkinje cell provides simultaneous access to complex spikes and simple spikes.
source: An extracellular recording from a Purkinje cell provides simultaneous access to two distinct physiological signals: complex spikes, which provide a one-to-one readout of spikes in the single climbing fiber innervating the Purkinje cell (Eccles et al., 1966); and simple spikes, which reflect the impact of all excitatory and inhibitory inputs as well as the intrinsic excitability of the Purkinje cell (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells in the flocculus encodes the retinal slip that drives VOR learning.
source: The climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells in the flocculus encodes the retinal slip that drives VOR learning (Simpson and Alley, 1974; Ghelarducci et al., 1975; Graf et al., 1988; Stone and Lisberger, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retinal slip can induce an adaptive increase or decrease in the gain of the VOR, depending on its direction relative to the vestibular stimulus.
source: Retinal slip can induce an adaptive increase or decrease in the gain of the VOR, depending on its direction relative to the vestibular stimulus (Boyden et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: To induce a learned increase in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction.
source: To induce a learned increase in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction (Figure 2A); to induce a learned decrease in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the same direction (Figure 2B; Collewijn and Grootendorst, 1979; Vercher and Gauthier, 1990–1991; Pastor et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1996).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: To induce a learned decrease in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the same direction.
source: To induce a learned increase in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction (Figure 2A); to induce a learned decrease in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the same direction (Figure 2B; Collewijn and Grootendorst, 1979; Vercher and Gauthier, 1990–1991; Pastor et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1996).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Most climbing fibers in the flocculus increase their firing in response to contraversive retinal slip.
source: Most climbing fibers in the flocculus increase their firing in response to contraversive retinal slip (image motion away from the side on which the cell is recorded) (Simpson and Alley, 1974; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Stone and Lisberger, 1990; Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli.
source: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,E), whereas during VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in the referenced figures.

claim: During VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli.
source: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,E), whereas during VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in the referenced figures.

claim: The amplitude of the climbing fiber response to retinal slip is the same during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.
source: The same climbing fibers encode retinal slip during both training paradigms, and the amplitude of the response is the same (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2E,F.

claim: What distinguishes VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training is whether the increased climbing fiber activity occurs during vestibular stimuli in one direction vs the other.
source: What distinguishes the two paradigms, and carries information about the required direction of learning, is whether the increased climbing fiber activity occurs during vestibular stimuli in one direction vs the other.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing the two training paradigms.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output, either through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (Ito et al., 1982) or through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell.
source: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output, either through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (Ito et al., 1982) or through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction in Purkinje cell firing during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli would cause VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei to receive inhibition from Purkinje cells that is more out-of-phase with the excitatory input they receive from vestibular afferents, leading to larger responses in the vestibular nuclei and an increase in VOR gain.
source: A reduction in Purkinje cell firing during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli would cause VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei to receive inhibition from Purkinje cells that is more out-of-phase with the excitatory input they receive from vestibular afferents (Figure 1), leading to larger responses in the vestibular nuclei and hence an increase in VOR gain (Ito, 1982).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A climbing fiber-triggered reduction in Purkinje cell firing during contraversive vestibular stimuli would cause the inhibition from Purkinje cells to be more in-phase with the excitatory vestibular afferents, resulting in smaller responses of vestibular nuclei neurons and a decrease in VOR gain.
source: In contrast, a climbing fiber-triggered reduction in Purkinje cell firing during contraversive vestibular stimuli would cause the inhibition from Purkinje cells to be more in-phase with the excitatory vestibular afferents, resulting in smaller responses of vestibular nuclei neurons and a decrease in VOR gain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on inference from the circuit architecture.

claim: Changes in Purkinje cell responses consistent with climbing fiber-triggered plasticity have been reported by several laboratories after VOR learning.
source: Such changes in Purkinje cell responses have been reported by several laboratories after VOR learning (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If there was a spike in the climbing fiber input on the first trial of a pair during VOR-increase training, there was a reduction of about 8 spikes/s in the firing rate of the Purkinje cell on the subsequent trial.
source: If there was a spike in the climbing fiber input on the first trial of a pair, there was a reduction of about 8 spikes/s in the firing rate of the Purkinje cell on the subsequent trial (Figure 3B,C; CF–No CF, red).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claim: On trials with no climbing fiber spike during VOR-increase training, there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing rate on the subsequent trial.
source: On trials with no climbing fiber spike, there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing rate on the subsequent trial (Figure 3B,C; No CF–No CF, black).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The sensory error (retinal slip speed) was indistinguishable on trials with a climbing fiber spike vs without a climbing fiber spike.
source: The sensory error (retinal slip speed) was indistinguishable on trials with a climbing fiber spike vs without a climbing fiber spike, and therefore cannot account for the difference observed on the trial after the climbing fiber spike (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of a climbing fiber spike on one trial and the change in Purkinje cell simple spike output on the next trial suggests that the activation of the climbing fibers is what is triggering the changes in Purkinje cell output during VOR-increase training.
source: The tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of a climbing fiber spike on one trial, and the change in Purkinje cell simple spike output on the next trial suggests that the activation of the climbing fibers is what is triggering the changes in Purkinje cell output during VOR-increase training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing on the trial after a climbing fiber spike during VOR-decrease training.
source: Unlike VOR-increase training and all previous trial-by-trial analyses of smooth pursuit learning (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2010, 2013), there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing on the trial after a climbing fiber spike during VOR-decrease training (Figure 3D,E; CF-No CF, blue).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The Purkinje cells underwent gradual, adaptive changes in their responses over the course of VOR-decrease training sessions.
source: The Purkinje cells did undergo gradual, adaptive changes in their responses over the course of the full VOR-decrease training session, which could be detected during the same ∼90-s VOR-decrease training sessions used for the trial-by-trial analysis (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Across trials of VOR-decrease training, there was a progressively lower Purkinje cell firing rate during contraversive vestibular stimuli.
source: Across trials of VOR-decrease training, there was a progressively lower Purkinje cell firing rate during contraversive vestibular stimuli, similar to what has been reported previously using much longer training periods (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles, Braitman, et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: Lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning.
source: This observation, along with the observation that lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning (Ito et al., 1982; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Lisberger et al., 1984; Nagao, 1983; Rambold and Churchland, 2002), indicates that the Purkinje cells in our sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Purkinje cells in the sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
source: This observation, along with the observation that lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning (Ito et al., 1982; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Lisberger et al., 1984; Nagao, 1983; Rambold and Churchland, 2002), indicates that the Purkinje cells in our sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and previous lesion studies.

claim: Although the performance errors elicited equally robust responses in the climbing fibers during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training, those responses seem to have a different impact in terms of their ability to induce plasticity.
source: Thus, although the performance errors elicited equally robust responses in the climbing fibers during the two learning paradigms, those responses seem to have a different impact in terms of their ability to induce plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing the two training paradigms.

claim: There is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli.
source: This seems unlikely because there is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Noda, 1986), and a substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli (Dufossé et al., 1978; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Miles et al., 1980; Watanabe, 1984; Nagao, 1989; Pastor et al, 1997; Lisberger et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1997; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Blazquez et al., 2003; Ke et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli.
source: This seems unlikely because there is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Noda, 1986), and a substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli (Dufossé et al., 1978; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Miles et al., 1980; Watanabe, 1984; Nagao, 1989; Pastor et al, 1997; Lisberger et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1997; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Blazquez et al., 2003; Ke et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There should be cerebellar synapses coactive with the climbing fibers during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training paradigms.
source: Thus, there should be cerebellar synapses coactive with the climbing fibers during both training paradigms, and therefore some other aspect of the state of the cerebellar circuit is more likely to be regulating the ability of the error signals carried by climbing fibers to induce plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous evidence about mossy fiber and Purkinje cell activity.

claim: When the number of spikelets and complex spike duration are manipulated in vitro or in decerebrate animals, the probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity can be altered, with shorter complex spike durations associated with a lower probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
source: When the number of spikelets, and hence the complex spike duration, is manipulated in vitro or in decerebrate animals (Carey and Regehr, 2009; Mathy et al., 2009; Rasmussen et al., 2013), the probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity can be altered, with shorter complex spike durations associated with a lower probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Complex spike waveforms during VOR-decrease training had more spikelets and were of longer duration than those during VOR-increase training.
source: Surprisingly, we found that complex spike waveforms during VOR-decrease training had more spikelets and were of longer duration than those during VOR-increase training (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: The reduced efficacy of climbing fibers to induce plasticity during VOR-decrease learning cannot be explained by a shorter complex spike duration.
source: Thus, the reduced efficacy of climbing fibers to induce plasticity during VOR-decrease learning cannot be explained by a shorter complex spike duration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on complex spike duration.

claim: There was no significant difference in the duration of the post-complex spike pause during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the duration of the post-complex spike pause during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: For both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to baseline during the training stimulus, but this reduction was smaller during VOR-decrease training than VOR-increase training.
source: For both, firing rate decreased relative to baseline during the training stimulus (Figure 2G,H), but this reduction was smaller during VOR-decrease training than VOR-increase training (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 2G,H and 5C.

claim: There is no floor effect limiting plasticity of the simple spike responses during VOR-decrease training.
source: This suggests that there is no floor effect limiting plasticity of the simple spike responses during VOR-decrease training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simple spike firing rate data.

claim: The difference in simple spike rates during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training suggests different patterns of excitatory and inhibitory input to Purkinje cells, which might regulate climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
source: Nevertheless, the difference in simple spike rates during the two training paradigms suggests different patterns of excitatory and inhibitory input to Purkinje cells, which might regulate climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the simple spike firing rate data.

claim: Virus carrying ChR2 was injected into the inferior olive to optogenetically stimulate climbing fibers.
source: To optogenetically stimulate climbing fibers, virus carrying ChR2 was injected into the inferior olive, and several weeks later, the climbing fiber terminals in the cerebellar flocculus were illuminated with blue light (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: ChR2 expression in the climbing fibers was verified anatomically, and optrode recordings from Purkinje cells demonstrated that complex spikes could be elicited by brief pulses of light to the flocculus.
source: ChR2 expression in the climbing fibers was verified anatomically, and optrode recordings from Purkinje cells demonstrated that complex spikes could be elicited by brief pulses of light to the flocculus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When climbing fibers were stimulated during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus, the VOR gain was higher than the vestibular-only control at the end of training.
source: If the climbing fibers were stimulated during the ipsiversive phase of the same vestibular stimulus, the VOR gain was higher than the vestibular-only control at the end of training (Figure 6B, red and Figure 7A, pink).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7A.

claim: The effect of climbing fiber stimulation during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus was long-lasting; when retested 2 hr after training, the VOR gain was still higher compared to vestibular-only training.
source: This effect of climbing fiber stimulation was long-lasting; when retested 2 hr after training, the VOR gain was still higher compared to vestibular-only training (Figure 6B, red and Figure 7B, pink).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7B.

claim: For both optogenetic VOR-increase and vestibular-only training paradigms, there was an increase in VOR gain between the end of training and the 2 hr retest, presumably reflecting decay of the non-associative habituation.
source: For both training paradigms, there was an increase in VOR gain between the end of training and the 2 hr retest, presumably reflecting decay of the non-associative habituation (Figure 6B, black and Figure 7, dark grey).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with a speculative explanation and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7.

claim: Pairing climbing fiber stimulation with the contraversive phase of the vestibular stimulus had no detectable effect on VOR gain, immediately or 2 hr post-training.
source: This pairing had no detectable effect, immediately or 2 hr post-training. There was no significant reduction of the gain of the VOR below the habituation level observed in response to training with the vestibular stimulus alone (Figure 6B, blue and Figure 7, light blue).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7.

claim: When the vestibular stimulus was paired with an appropriate visual stimulus, there was a bigger decrease in VOR gain than induced by the vestibular stimulus alone, demonstrating that an associative decrease in VOR gain was possible.
source: In contrast, when the vestibular stimulus was paired with an appropriate visual stimulus (see 'Materials and methods'), there was a bigger decrease in VOR gain than induced by the vestibular stimulus alone, demonstrating that an associative decrease in VOR gain was possible (Figure 7A, white).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Stronger climbing fiber stimulation paradigms (three stimuli per cycle, unilateral or bilateral) induced bigger increases in VOR gain when delivered during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus.
source: These stronger climbing fiber stimulation paradigms induced bigger increases in VOR gain when delivered during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus (Figure 7, dark pink and red).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: When timed to induce VOR-decrease learning, increasing the number of climbing fiber stimuli had no effect.
source: However, when timed to induce VOR-decrease learning, increasing the number of climbing fiber stimuli had no effect (Figure 7, blue and dark blue).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: None of the optogenetic training paradigms induced a decrease in VOR gain below the vestibular-only control, either immediately or 2 hr after the end of training.
source: Thus, none of our training paradigms induced a decrease in VOR gain below the vestibular-only control, either immediately or 2 hr after the end of training.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The same climbing fiber stimulation protocols were effective at inducing robust and graded learning when timed relative to the vestibular stimulus to mimic VOR-increase training.
source: However, the same climbing fiber stimulation protocols were effective at inducing robust and graded learning when timed relative to the vestibular stimulus to mimic VOR-increase training.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The lack of VOR-decrease learning in response to optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation was consistent with the trial-by-trial analysis, which found no evidence for a contribution of the natural, visually-elicited error signals in the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-decrease learning.
source: Moreover, the lack of VOR-decrease learning in response to optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation was consistent with the trial-by-trial analysis, which found no evidence for a contribution of the natural, visually-elicited error signals in the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the optogenetic stimulation results with the trial-by-trial analysis results.

claim: The stimulation results, together with the trial-by-trial recordings, suggest that VOR-decrease learning is not induced by the climbing fibers, even though they carry error signals that could potentially guide learning.
source: Thus, the stimulation results, together with the trial-by-trial recordings, suggest that VOR-decrease learning is not induced by the climbing fibers, even though they carry error signals that could potentially guide learning, and the very same climbing fibers contribute to the induction of VOR-increase learning.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: Both recording and stimulation results indicate that during VOR learning, the efficacy of the climbing fibers for inducing plasticity is gated downstream of their encoding of errors.
source: Both our recording and stimulation results indicate that during VOR learning, the efficacy of the climbing fibers for inducing plasticity is gated downstream of their encoding of errors.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: The coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity is regulated, and can vary across different learning contexts.
source: In contrast, a comparison of the positive and negative results from the two VOR learning paradigms indicates that the coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity is regulated, and can vary across different learning contexts.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.

claim: The results provide some of the strongest evidence to date that error signals carried by the climbing fibers drive VOR-increase learning.
source: Our results provide some of the strongest evidence to date that error signals carried by the climbing fibers drive VOR-increase learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results for VOR-increase training.

claim: The equally robust error signals carried by the climbing fibers during VOR-decrease training seem to make little or no contribution to the induction of learning.
source: However, the equally robust error signals carried by the climbing fibers during VOR-decrease training seem to make little or no contribution to the induction of learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results for VOR-decrease training.

claim: During VOR-decrease training, the animals are learning.
source: During VOR-decrease training, the animals are learning (Raymond and Lisberger, 1996), and there are changes in the responses of the Purkinje cells that can be detected within the 90-s training period (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The changes in Purkinje cell responses during VOR-decrease training do not seem to be driven by the climbing fibers.
source: However, those changes do not seem to be driven by the climbing fibers, because there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in Purkinje cell simple spike responses of the kind observed during VOR-increase or smooth pursuit learning (Figure 3, Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial-by-trial analysis results.

claim: In vivo, climbing fiber activity is sometimes a potent trigger for plasticity, but at other times has no effect.
source: Thus, in vivo, climbing fiber activity is sometimes a potent trigger for plasticity, but at other times has no effect.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.

claim: Gating of the climbing fibers' efficacy for inducing plasticity represents a novel component of the cerebellar learning algorithm.
source: This gating of the climbing fibers' efficacy for inducing plasticity represents a novel component of the cerebellar learning algorithm.
evidence: This is a main conclusion and interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The convergent evidence from recording and stimulation experiments, as well as previous perturbation studies, strengthens the interpretation of the results.
source: The convergent evidence from recording and stimulation experiments, as well as previous, perturbation studies, strengthens the interpretation of the results.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach and interpretation of the study.

claim: The current recording and stimulation results are consistent with a previous perturbation study reporting that mice with impaired pf-Pk LTD are selectively impaired on VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning.
source: Moreover, the current recording and stimulation results are consistent with a previous perturbation study reporting that mice with impaired long-term depression of the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD) are selectively impaired on VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning (Boyden et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The present results extend previous work by demonstrating a selective contribution, not only of pf-Pk LTD, but of all climbing fiber-dependent plasticity mechanisms to VOR-increase learning but not VOR-decrease learning.
source: Thus, the present results extend our previous work by demonstrating a selective contribution, not only of pf-Pk LTD, but of all climbing fiber-dependent plasticity mechanisms to VOR-increase learning but not VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and their interpretation.

claim: The results for VOR-increase learning provide a positive control indicating that the experimental approaches were able to detect climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
source: The results for VOR-increase learning provide a positive control indicating that our experimental approaches were able to detect climbing fiber-triggered plasticity, which is critical for interpreting the negative results from VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and interpretation.

claim: Direct comparison of the VOR-increase and VOR-decrease paradigms provides a demonstration that the very same animals and even the very same cells could toggle between either a tight coupling or no apparent coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity, depending on the behavioral context.
source: In contrast, direct comparison of the VOR-increase and VOR-decrease paradigms provides a demonstration that the very same animals and even the very same cells could toggle between either a tight coupling or no apparent coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity, depending on the behavioral context of the specific oculomotor training paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Direct comparison of the positive and negative results from VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning in the same animals and the same cells, using the same techniques, suggests that climbing fiber efficacy is actively regulated.
source: Thus, direct comparison of the positive and negative results from VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning in the same animals and the same cells, using the same techniques, suggests that climbing fiber efficacy is actively regulated.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In vitro, ethanol and neuromodulators such as norepinephrine can affect the duration of a complex spike and the induction of climbing fiber-dependent plasticity.
source: In vitro, ethanol and neuromodulators such as norepinephrine can affect the duration of a complex spike and the induction of climbing fiber-dependent plasticity (Carey and Regehr 2009; He et al., 2013; Belmeguenai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There was no reduction in complex spike duration during VOR-decrease training that would account for the reduced efficacy of climbing fiber spikes suggested by the trial-by-trial analysis.
source: However, there was no reduction in complex spike duration during VOR-decrease training that would account for the reduced efficacy of climbing fiber spikes suggested by the trial-by-trial analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on complex spike duration.

claim: Coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Another factor that may gate the efficacy of climbing fibers to induce synaptic plasticity is the level of inhibition: coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (Ekerot and Kano, 1985), but also may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibitory inputs may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
source: Another factor that may gate the efficacy of climbing fibers to induce synaptic plasticity is the level of inhibition: coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (Ekerot and Kano, 1985), but also may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training paradigms, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to the spontaneous, pre-stimulus baseline around the time of climbing fiber activation.
source: During both training paradigms, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to the spontaneous, pre-stimulus baseline around the time of climbing fiber activation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The decrease in simple spike rate was smaller during VOR-decrease than VOR-increase training, indicating a higher ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cells at the time of climbing fiber activity during VOR-decrease vs VOR-increase training.
source: This decrease in simple spike rate was smaller during VOR-decrease than VOR-increase training, indicating a higher ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cells at the time of climbing fiber activity during VOR-decrease vs VOR-increase training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simple spike firing rate data.

claim: The results provide some of the first evidence that the changes observed over different time scales may be mechanistically related, by showing parallels between the contribution, or lack of a contribution, of climbing fiber activity to plasticity on different time scales: a single trial, over the course of a 30-min training session, and 2 hr after the end of training.
source: Our results provide some of the first evidence that the changes observed over different time scales may be mechanistically related, by showing parallels between the contribution, or lack of a contribution, of climbing fiber activity to plasticity on different time scales: a single trial, over the course of a 30-min training session, and 2 hr after the end of training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results across different time scales.

claim: In the trial-by-trial analysis for VOR-increase training, the change in Purkinje cell activity on trials following a climbing fiber spike was approximately 10% of the average firing rate.
source: In the trial-by-trial analysis for VOR-increase training, the change in Purkinje cell activity on trials following a climbing fiber spike was remarkably large, approximately 10% of the average firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The direction of the trial-by-trial changes in Purkinje cell responses during VOR-increase learning are consistent with those observed over the course of a brief, 90 s VOR-increase training period and those observed after several hours or days of VOR-increase training.
source: In particular, the direction of the trial-by-trial changes in Purkinje cell responses during VOR-increase learning are consistent with those observed over the course of a brief, 90 s VOR-increase training period (Figures 3B and 4, red) and those observed after several hours or days of VOR-increase training (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and references to figures.

claim: The results from the trial-by-trial analysis were consistent with the changes observed over tens of minutes to hours in the stimulation experiments, in that both suggested a contribution of the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning.
source: Moreover, our results from the trial-by-trial analysis were consistent with the changes we observed over tens of minutes to hours in the stimulation experiments (Figures 6 and 7), in that both suggested a contribution of the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results across different experimental approaches and time scales.

claim: The results provide evidence for a novel component of the neural algorithm for cerebellar learning in vivo—namely, a gating of the ability of error signals in the climbing fibers to induce learning.
source: Our results provide evidence for a novel component of the neural algorithm for cerebellar learning in vivo—namely, a gating of the ability of error signals in the climbing fibers to induce learning.
evidence: This is a main conclusion and interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Previous work has shown that regulation can occur at the level of olivary spiking.
source: Since previous work has shown that regulation can also occur at the level of olivary spiking, climbing fiber-triggered plasticity seems to be gated at two different stages—at the level of the olivary neurons responding to a performance error by either spiking or not spiking, and at the level of climbing fiber spikes either inducing or not inducing plasticity.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Climbing fiber-triggered plasticity seems to be gated at two different stages—at the level of the olivary neurons responding to a performance error by either spiking or not spiking, and at the level of climbing fiber spikes either inducing or not inducing plasticity.
source: Since previous work has shown that regulation can also occur at the level of olivary spiking, climbing fiber-triggered plasticity seems to be gated at two different stages—at the level of the olivary neurons responding to a performance error by either spiking or not spiking, and at the level of climbing fiber spikes either inducing or not inducing plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings combined with previous work.

claim: The cerebellum appears to conditionally heed the instructive signals provided by the climbing fibers.
source: Thus, the cerebellum appears to conditionally heed the instructive signals provided by the climbing fibers.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Dynamic gating of the neural error signals controlling the induction of learning may be a general feature of neural learning algorithms.
source: Dynamic gating of the neural error signals controlling the induction of learning may be a general feature of neural learning algorithms, and merits systematic investigation in the cerebellum and other circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the study's findings.

claim: Defining the factors that influence the receptivity of the cerebellum to neural error signals will be critical for developing more sophisticated theories of learning, and for developing strategies to optimize the recruitment of plasticity to aid learning or recovery from injury.
source: Defining the factors that influence the receptivity of the cerebellum to neural error signals will be critical for developing more sophisticated theories of learning, and for developing strategies to optimize the recruitment of plasticity to aid learning or recovery from injury.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications and future directions of the research.
